headline_marked: [[Bill Gates features Bangladeshi scientist Firdausi Qadri]] in video on cholera vaccine
headline: Bill Gates features Bangladeshi scientist Firdausi Qadri in video on cholera vaccine
summary: Tech mogul Bill Gates highlighted Dr. Firdausi Qadri's work on oral cholera vaccines, emphasizing their critical role in preventing outbreaks in vulnerable regions like Bangladesh. His video coincides with a major vaccination drive across high-risk areas.
details: On October 7, technology entrepreneur Bill Gates released a video across his social media platforms, including Facebook and LinkedIn, discussing the cholera vaccine. This video highlights the significant efforts in cholera prevention.

Many in Bangladesh may have already received their first dose of the oral cholera vaccine, as a large-scale vaccination program has been underway. The first dose was administered from August 22 to September 26.

This program targeted 14 high-risk areas in Dhaka, Kishoreganj, Narayanganj, Munshiganj, and Brahmanbaria. The vaccine is available for everyone over one year old, excluding pregnant women, and two doses are required for full protection.
The second dose is being given from September 26 to October 25 at various schools and local health centers. More details on vaccination sites and schedules are available on vaxepi.gov.bd.

In his video, Bill Gates explained that cholera is a severe diarrheal disease primarily spread through contaminated water, which can be rapidly fatal without timely treatment. He specifically mentioned Bangladeshi scientist Firdausi Qadri for her work in using this vaccine to halt cholera outbreaks.

Cholera risk is higher in densely populated countries like Bangladesh, where access to safe drinking water and improved sanitation is limited. While long-term prevention requires robust water and sanitation systems, these are time-consuming and expensive to establish.

This is where the cholera vaccine plays a crucial role, offering rapid disease prevention. It is easy to produce, affordable, and administered orally instead of by injection, making it highly accessible.
Bill Gates further praised Dr. Qadri and her fellow researchers, stating that their work on this easily acceptable vaccine is saving countless lives by preventing a deadly disease like cholera.

Dr. Firdausi Qadri noted that Bangladesh has a national cholera control plan detailing when and where vaccines should be administered. Implementing this plan and its roadmap requires approximately 100 million vaccine doses.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has long supported the innovation and research of low-cost oral cholera vaccines in Bangladesh, collaborating with icddr,b and Firdausi Qadri to make affordable vaccines accessible. Gates' video is part of this awareness campaign.

Dr. Firdausi Qadri is an internationally renowned researcher, head of the Mucosal Immunology and Vaccinology Unit at icddr,b, and a recipient of the Independence Award (2013) and the Ramon Magsaysay Award (2021). This is not the first time Bill Gates has featured her work, having previously highlighted her contributions on his blog and website, GatesNotes.

headline_marked: [[Measles vaccine for 6 months to 9-year-olds]] recommended within 2 weeks on priority
headline: Measles vaccine for 6 months to 9-year-olds recommended within 2 weeks on priority
summary: A joint independent evaluation team has recommended urgent vaccination for children aged 6 months to 9 years to combat a measles outbreak in Bangladesh, urging priority for high-infection districts.
details: A joint independent evaluation team has recommended priority vaccination for children aged six months to nine years within two weeks to tackle the ongoing measles outbreak in Bangladesh. The team specifically urged prioritizing districts with high infection rates and a large number of unvaccinated children.

These recommendations were presented at a workshop in Dhaka by the 70-member joint independent evaluation team, which comprises national and international experts. The team was formed as part of a review of the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) and surveillance of vaccine-preventable diseases.

According to the team, a "measles outbreak explosion" has occurred in Bangladesh due to various vaccination failures. These include a significant number of children missed from vaccination between 2000 and 2025, the projected depletion of measles-rubella vaccine stock by 2025, and the exclusion of children over two years from routine vaccination.

The outbreak, which began in March, shows no signs of abating, despite a national measles-rubella vaccination campaign conducted from April 5 to May 20. Although the health department continued routine vaccinations and covered missed children, the outbreak has not been brought under control.

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) reported seven deaths and 1,319 new measles cases in the 24 hours leading up to Sunday morning. Since March 15, a total of 236,366 patients have been hospitalized with measles symptoms, and 1,196 deaths have been recorded.

Experts also recommended vaccinating health workers and administering the measles-rubella vaccine at six months of age until the outbreak ends. They emphasized maintaining the highest standards in measles surveillance and outbreak response, including proper documentation of suspected cases.

Further recommendations include updating local vaccination plans to include chronically missed populations and verifying vaccination cards during school admissions. The team also advised extending the maximum age for routine vaccination from two to five years and planning the next national measles-rubella campaign in a timely manner.
